questions.q: Why do commercial TV episodes end each act on a turn or cliffhanger?
choices: To keep viewers watching through the commercial break
questions.explain: The act-out exists because of advertising.

questions.q: A writer pitches a series but can only think of three episodes. What's probably missing?
choices: An engine that keeps generating stories
questions.explain: A series needs a situation, such as cases through the door or an unresolvable relationship, that produces stories for years.

choices: It drops us into a world already running, like a typical episode
It shows the series' situation beginning
questions.explain: A premise pilot has a built-in story but may not look like later episodes.

questions.q: In an episode, the C story is usually…
choices: The main plot carried by the lead
A secondary plot for other characters
A small thread or running joke
questions.explain: A runner, sometimes just a recurring gag across a few scenes.

questions.q: A show closes a case each week while slowly advancing a conspiracy over the season. This is…
choices: A hybrid of episodic and serialized storytelling
questions.explain: The X-Files' split between 'monster of the week' and 'mythology' episodes is the classic example.

questions.q: What's the danger in resolving a series' engine?
choices: The show may lose the thing that generates its stories
questions.explain: If the couple gets together or the secret comes out, the series may stall unless a new engine replaces it.

questions.q: What is a common criticism of fully serialized streaming seasons?
choices: They can feel like stretched films with episodes that don't stand alone
questions.explain: Critics call it the 'ten-hour movie' problem.

ideas: Each act should end on a small cliffhanger so the audience comes back after the break.
A good series needs an engine, a situation that generates new stories week after week.
An episode interweaves a main A story with secondary B and C stories that echo its theme.
